title: The last disciple
hookLine: the wanderer Subhadda is turned away at the door; the Buddha calls him in (DN 16)
last: REST IS PART OF THE PATH.

cards: Arriving just as the doors close. The store's locking up. Visiting hours ended five minutes ago.

Someone behind the glass shakes their head: sorry, too late. In Kusinara that night, word goes around: the teacher Gotama will pass away in the last watch of the night. A wandering seeker named Subhadda hears it.
He's not a follower; he belongs to another group of wanderers. But a question has been nagging at him for years, and he thinks this teacher might be the one who can clear it up. Now or never.
So he hurries out to the sal grove, in the dark.

teach.b: At the edge of the grove, Subhadda meets Ananda and asks: may I see the teacher? Ananda, loyal, exhausted, grieving, says: enough, friend Subhadda. Don't trouble him.
He's weary. Subhadda asks again. No.
A third time. No. You can understand Ananda completely; he's protecting someone he loves in his last hours.
But the Buddha, lying between the trees, hears them. Enough, Ananda, he says. Don't keep Subhadda out.
Let him come. Whatever he asks, he'll ask because he wants to understand, not to bother me. So Subhadda comes in, sits, and asks.
All these well-known teachers, heads of big schools, each says he's found the truth. Have they all really understood? Or none of them?
Or some? The Buddha waves the comparison away. Let that be, Subhadda.
Never mind them. I'll teach you the thing itself. Wherever the noble eightfold path is found, there you'll find people who truly practice it and reach its fruits.
Subhadda asks to go forth, right there, and the Buddha asks Ananda to ordain him. The text says that, living earnestly, not long after, Subhadda reached the goal.
He was the last person the Buddha taught directly.
Notice who got in. Not a longtime monk. An outsider from another group, arriving after hours with a question.
And the dying teacher overrode his own protective attendant to make room. The door wasn't closed yet.

how: Buddhists remember Subhadda as the last disciple the Buddha personally taught, and the story is often told to show that the door to the teaching stays open to anyone who asks sincerely.

o: a rival teacher who came to debate the Buddha
the Buddha's cousin and lifelong attendant
the last disciple the Buddha taught himself

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.

s: Ananda let Subhadda in right away
he refused three times, protecting his tired teacher.
Subhadda came from another group of wanderers
an outsider, arriving in the last hours.
the Buddha answered by ranking the other teachers
he set the comparison aside and taught the path itself.

games.q: you're dying, and you hear your attendant turning away a stranger with a sincere question. what do you do?
o: send a short message and rest.
games.why: he says: enough, Ananda. let him come. Subhadda becomes the last person the Buddha taught directly.

practice: Think of someone who shows up late in your life: the friend who always texts after the plans are set, the person who joined the team last, or a question you keep putting off because it came at a bad time.
Picture the door, your hand on it, about to close. Then open it a little wider; there's room.

wordCard.voice: Subhadda. The wanderer turned away three times at the door, and called in by the dying Buddha himself, the last disciple he taught.

orig.note: Pali: a name meaning auspicious, fortunate. Su (good) and bhadda (blessed).

carryVoice: Your line: there's still time. Turned away three times, and still he got in. Eighty-three days, and counting.
